rows.verified: HSE defines work-related violence as abuse, threats or assault occurring in circumstances related to work, including verbal, online and telephone abuse.
Employers must protect workers from work-related violence so far as reasonably practicable and include it within health and safety management.
Employers must assess significant violence risks, consult workers and implement effective controls rather than treating the assessment as an end in itself.
Where violence risk cannot be removed, employers should combine workplace design, security, work-practice, communication and training controls.
Training can cover warning signs, communication, de-escalation, work practices and incident-reporting procedures, with periodic refresher training.
After work-related violence, employers should support affected workers, record and report applicable incidents and review whether controls need improvement.
RIDDOR reporting can be required where work-related violence causes death, a specified injury or an over-seven-day worker incapacity.
Workers should use provided information and training, report violence or aggression and raise unresolved safety concerns through workplace channels.
Violence controls depend on work activity, client or public interaction, lone working, time, location, cash or valuables, worker vulnerability and incident history.
Workplace-violence evidence is activity-, worker- and context-specific and is not an exact parcel-level assault probability.
Employers have a legal duty to protect workers from work-related stress by assessing the risk and acting on the findings.
HSE identifies six main work-design areas linked to stress: demands, control, support, relationships, role and change.
The Management Standards provide a structured risk-assessment approach focused on underlying causes and practical improvements.
Work demands should be adequate and achievable, matched to workers' skills and abilities, with concerns about the work environment addressed.
Where possible workers should have a say over pace, methods, use of skills, development opportunities, breaks and work patterns.
Organisations should provide accessible support systems, resources, manager and colleague support and regular constructive feedback.
Organisations should make roles and responsibilities clear, avoid incompatible requirements and provide ways to raise role conflicts.
Employers must assess mental as well as physical work risks and share relevant risk-assessment outcomes with workers.
Stress controls depend on work design, workload, autonomy, support, relationships, organisational change, worker needs and existing health conditions.
Work-related-stress evidence is organisation-, role- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level mental-health probability.
